processing: A flat-shaped green tea: the leaf is heated to stop oxidation, then pressed flat and dried. A pressed tea-cake version also exists, and its making was listed as Sichuan provincial intangible heritage in 2014.
harvest_season: Specific picking dates are not well recorded. As with other Sichuan greens, the early spring harvest is the one to look for.
appearance_dry: Flat, straight, smooth and pointed leaves with a glossy deep green colour.
appearance_wet: Even, bright leaves, thick for a green tea.
taste_profile: Fresh and mellow with a returning sweetness, and a high lasting aroma described as orchid or chestnut. The thick leaf holds up well to repeat steeps.

brewing.notes: Flat teas float at first, so give them a moment to sink. Pour off fully between steeps so the leaf does not stew.

vintage_note: Sold like other Chinese greens, as the current year's spring tea, best drunk within about a year. The protected name covers 32 townships of Qingchuan County, so ask where in the county it was made. The pressed cake is a separate, heritage-minded product.
description:
Qifo Gongcha is a flat green tea from Qingchuan County in the north of Sichuan, named for Qifo township and for its old reputation as a tribute tea. Gardens in the township sit between 580 and 2100 metres, averaging around 800, in misty and heavily wooded hills.

The finished leaf is flat, straight and pointed, closer in shape to a Long Jing style tea than to the curly greens of the region. The leaf is noticeably thick, which gives the cup more body than its pale colour suggests.

In the cup it is fresh and mellow with a sweet finish, and the aroma is described as orchid or chestnut. Keep the water around 85°C and the first steep to about a minute; hotter or longer brings out bitterness faster than it brings out flavour.

The name has had national geographical indication protection since 2008, covering all 32 townships then in Qingchuan County. That is much wider than Qifo itself, so a label alone does not mean the tea came from the namesake township. Buy the current spring harvest and ask for the place of origin.
history:
Local accounts say Qifo tea was sent as tribute in the Tang dynasty, and a popular legend has Empress Wu Zetian appointing tea officials and establishing a tribute garden here. These stories are repeated widely but are best read as tradition.

Firmer ground comes later: the Zhaohua county gazetteer records a 1947 order from Deng Xihou, then chair of Sichuan province, praising the tribute tea of Dafotan, the place now called Qifo. National geographical indication status followed on 7 May 2008, and the tea-cake technique entered Sichuan's provincial intangible heritage list in 2014.
